title: First Light
subtitle: Your first Aktion program, from nothing

intro.headline: A program is a list of statements. That's it.
intro.body:
Aktion looks like JavaScript because it *is* a strict subset of it — `function`, `if`, arrow functions, object literals, all the operators you already know. What it adds is a rule about where the UI comes from.

Every program renders from one place: `$app(...)`. The runtime streams your statements in, top to bottom, committing each line the moment it arrives — so the page shell appears before its contents finish loading.

In this world you will write a complete, valid Aktion program without learning a single new keyword.
objectives: Find the render root in any program
Build a component tree with `Column` and `Text`
Order a program so the shell streams first
Spot the two roots that *look* right and aren't
Write a valid program from an empty file

stages.title: The one entry point
stages.goal: Every Aktion program renders from exactly one $app(...).

teach.text:
There is no `main`, no `export default`, no `ReactDOM.render`. There is `$app(...)`, and there is **exactly one per program**.

Whatever you pass it becomes the page. It accepts a single node, an array of nodes rendered as siblings, or several nodes as separate arguments.

Everything else in the file — variables, functions, effects — exists to feed that one call.

code.caption: three ways to call it, one per program

tips: `$app` is a *builtin*, not a component — it never appears inside a tree.

tips.text: `aktion = Column([...])` is the pre-0.5 root form. The parser still tolerates it, so the validator stays silent — but nothing renders.

challenge.title: Which line renders the page?
challenge.prompt: One of these puts UI on the screen. The other three are ordinary statements that happen to build components.

options.detail: A perfectly valid statement — it just names a tree.
The legacy root form. Parses, renders nothing.

hints: Three of these are assignments. Only one is a call to a builtin.
Look for the `$` sigil — builtins always carry it.
stages.explain: `$app(...)` is the reserved entry point and the only thing that mounts UI. `page = ...` builds a tree and parks it under a name — useful, but inert until `$app` receives it. `aktion = ...` is the pre-0.5 root that the parser still accepts, which makes it the most dangerous of the three: it validates cleanly and renders nothing.

codex.def: The reserved render root. Exactly one per program; whatever you pass it becomes the page.

stages.title: Trees, not markup
stages.goal: Build UI by nesting component calls inside arrays.

teach.text:
There is no JSX and no template syntax. A UI is a **function call whose arguments are more function calls**.

Containers take an array of children. Leaves take their content. That is the entire composition model:

code.src:
$app(Column([
  PageHeader("Inbox"),
  Card([
    Text("3 unread"),
    Button("Mark all read")
  ])
]))
code.caption: arrays nest as deep as you like

parts.text: the one call that mounts the page
children always arrive as an array
a container inside a container — no depth limit

tips: PascalCase names are components; they return trees.
Reach for a pattern composite like `PageHeader` before hand-building the same thing out of `Row` + `Text`.

challenge.title: Complete the program
challenge.prompt: Drop the right tokens into the slots. Two of the chips are things a React developer would reach for — leave those in the bank.

hints: The outermost call is always the same one.
`PageHeader` is the page-level title composite; `Text` is the plain paragraph.
stages.explain: Composition is just nesting calls. `Column` takes an array, and each entry in that array is another component call. Note what is *not* here: no wrapper element, no `className`, no fragment. The tree is the markup.

afterCode.src:
$app(Column([
  PageHeader("Welcome back"),
  Text("You have 3 new orders")
]))
afterCode.caption: the shape to remember

codex.def: Nested component calls where containers take an array of children. No JSX, no templates — just calls.

preview.program:
$app(Column([
  PageHeader("Welcome back", { subtitle: "You have 3 new orders" }),
  Card([Text("Everything on this card came from four lines of Aktion.")])
]))

stages.title: Shell first, leaves later
stages.goal: Put $app(...) at the top and reference names defined below it.

teach.text:
The renderer commits each statement **as it streams in**. So the order you write things changes what the user sees first.

Names resolve from the whole top-level scope, not from source order — so `$app` can reference a `header` that is defined ten lines further down. That is the point: call `$app(...)` first and the page shell appears immediately, then each detail fills in as its line arrives.

Writing `$app` last means the user stares at nothing until the entire program has downloaded.

code.src:
$app(Column([header, stats, table]))

header = PageHeader("Orders")
stats  = Stats([StatCard("Revenue", { value: "$48k" })])
table  = Card([Text("…")])
code.caption: forward references are the idiom, not a hack

columns.title: Root last
columns.note: Nothing on screen until the last line lands.

columns.title: Root first
columns.note: Shell paints immediately; leaves attach as they arrive.

tips.text: This is a *streaming* concern, not a correctness one. Both orders produce the same final page — one just feels instant.

challenge.title: Order the program
challenge.prompt: Arrange these four statements so the page shell commits as early as possible, then each section fills in.

hints: Which single line is the one the reconciler needs before it can attach anything?
After the root, keep the sections in the order they appear on screen.
stages.explain: Hoisting is what makes this work — references resolve from the entire top-level scope, so `$app` naming `header` before `header` exists is not a forward-declaration trick, it's the normal way to write Aktion. Root first gives the reconciler a shell to attach streamed leaves to.

codex.def: Statements commit as they arrive. Call $app(...) first and forward-reference the sections below it so the shell paints immediately.

stages.title: Root Lock
stages.goal: Feel the streaming rule instead of reading it.

teach.text:
Statements are falling. The bar at the bottom is the render root.

**Catch `$app(page)` before anything else.** A leaf that lands before the shell has nothing to attach to — which is exactly what happens in a real program when you put `$app` last.

Once the root is locked, bank five more statements to clear the stage.
tips: Move the mouse — or drag on a touch screen — to slide the bar.

challenge.title: Catch the root first
challenge.prompt: Catch `$app(page)` first, then bank five more statements. Anything you catch before the root ends the run.
challenge.note: Move the pointer to slide the render root. Missed statements just fall away — only order matters.

fallback.prompt: Why does putting `$app(...)` on the first line matter?

options.label: The page shell commits immediately, and later statements attach to it as they stream in.
Names defined below it would otherwise be undefined.
options.detail: References resolve from the whole top-level scope — order does not affect resolution.

options.label: The parser requires it.
options.detail: It does not; $app can sit anywhere.

hints: The gold chip is the root. Everything cyan is a leaf.
Miss the root on purpose if you have to — it comes back around.
stages.explain: In a real streaming render this is exactly the failure: `$app` arrives last, so every earlier statement is a component with nowhere to mount, and the user watches a blank page until the final byte. Root first, always.

codex.def: The renderer attaches each statement the moment it parses, so the shell must arrive before the leaves that hang off it.

stages.title: The root that isn't
stages.goal: Recognise the two roots that validate but render nothing.

teach.text:
The schema validator is good at unknown props and misspelled components. It is powerless against a program that is *structurally fine and semantically wrong*.

Two failures produce a completely blank page with a completely clean validator:

- **`aktion = ...`** — the pre-0.5 root binding. Still parses. Never renders.
- **A component with no `return`** — the body runs, builds nothing, renders nothing.

Both of these are silent. When a page is mysteriously empty, check for them first.

infographic.title: Silent failures
rows: Two roots — only one program allowed

tips.text: A missing `return` is the single most common cause of "my component disappeared".

challenge.title: Find the silent failure
challenge.prompt: This program validates cleanly and renders an empty page. Tap the token responsible.

hints: Both bugs are here, but only one is the token that stops *anything at all* from mounting.
Ask which name the runtime actually looks for when it decides what to render.
stages.explain: `aktion = ...` is the pre-0.5 root form. The parser tolerates it for backwards compatibility, so nothing complains — but the runtime mounts `$app(...)` and only `$app(...)`, so the page stays empty. (The missing `return` in `Greeting` is a real second bug; fix that too, and note that it would have cost you only that one component instead of the whole page.)

afterCode.caption: the root the runtime looks for

codex.def: `aktion = ...` is the pre-0.5 render root. It still parses, so the validator stays quiet — but only `$app(...)` mounts.

stages.title: From an empty file
stages.goal: Write a complete, valid Aktion program with no scaffold.

teach.text:
Everything you need is now on the table: one root, nested calls, arrays for children.

Write a program that renders a page with a heading and a line of body text. Any components from the library are fair game — `PageHeader`, `Card`, `Text`, `Button`, `Callout` all work — as long as the whole thing hangs off a single `$app(...)`.

If the real Aktion language service is reachable, it will check your program for real and print its diagnostics under the editor.

challenge.title: Write it yourself
challenge.prompt: Render a page: a `PageHeader` with any title, and a `Text` under it. Everything must be inside one `$app(...)` and stacked in a `Column`.

mustWhy: The two pieces need a Column([ ... ]) to stack them.
Add a PageHeader with a title string.
Add a Text with some body copy.

hints: Open with `$app(` and close it at the very end.
stages.explain: That is a complete, shippable Aktion program. No build step, no imports, no component registration — the library is already in scope and `$app` is the only ceremony. Every world from here on adds behaviour to this same shape.

codex.def: One `$app(...)` wrapping a container wrapping components. Nothing else is required.

preview.program:
$app(Column([
  PageHeader("Orders", { subtitle: "Everything shipped this month" }),
  Card([Text("You just wrote this. It is running for real.")])
]))

outro.headline: You can write Aktion now
outro.body: One root, nested calls, arrays for children, shell first. Everything else in this arcade is behaviour layered onto that shape.
outro.nextHint: Next: Reactive Pulse — make the page change without writing a single re-render.
